# Softanza Radar

> What changed in AI and the tech field this week, and what it means for what we build in Softanza. Softanza Radar reads the week's papers, releases, security findings and practices at their source, judges each one from Softanza's point of view, and tells us, the Softanza team, what it means for us and what we should do about it: a check to run, a lesson to learn, or work proposed to the part it concerns.

Every file below is plain data or plain text. The two feed files are signed with SSH (Ed25519, namespace radar-feed, signer feed@radar): check a signature before trusting a feed.

## Feeds
- [Feed index](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/feed/index.json): every entry as data; its signature is feed/index.json.sig, its contract docs/FEED.md
- [JSON Feed 1.1](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/feed/feed.json): the same entries for feed readers; signature feed/feed.json.sig
- [Signer key](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/keys/allowed_signers): the public key both signatures are checked against
- [Configuration](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/app/config.json): the project, its readers, its stances and where its map is
- [Map](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/map/estate.json): the project's layers, parts, domains and concerns

## Signals, newest first
- [Together AI distils Kimi-K3.1-Pro's Lao translation into Qwen3.8-27B for $260 in all, from 4,000 teacher translations, reaching 93% of the teacher's score while a language it was not trained on holds](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-27-distilling-kimi-into-qwen.md): advice, practice, adopt, 2026-11-27. Together AI (Zain Hasan and Sonny Khan, November 26, 2026) taught Qwen3.8-27B to translate English into Lao from Kimi-K3.1-Pro's own translations. The two models use different tokenizers, so the teacher passes only text: it translates FLORES-200 and Wikipedia sentences at temperature 0 with thinking off, a filter keeps translations written at least 70% in the target script, and the student is trained on them with LoRA and cross-entropy on its own chat template. On chrF++ the student's Lao rises from 5.5 to 44.3, against 47.5 for the teacher, and its Thai, mixed into the data, rises from 46.7 to 47.8; training on 945 human Lao references alone scores 44.7 on Lao and drops Thai to 5.3. The teacher's 4,000 Lao translations cost $7.46 and all the experiments $260. A five-language adapter raised Northern Sotho from 32.7 to 48.0 and Zulu from 37.7 to 39.2. The figures are the authors' own.
- [llm.asm runs Qwen3-0.6B from 17,252 lines of x86-64 assembly, as a 14.7 KB Linux program with no libc and as a 24 KB kernel booted by GRUB; it states decode speeds above llama.cpp's on the same processor](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-26-llm-asm-bare-metal.md): advice, release, learn, 2026-11-26. llm.asm (MIT, published by alesha-pro on November 25, 2026) runs the full 28-layer forward pass of Qwen3-0.6B, with its BPE tokenizer, in NASM assembly. It comes as a static Linux program of 14,712 bytes that uses raw system calls and no libc, and as a bare-metal kernel of 24,252 bytes booted by GRUB through Multiboot, with VGA text, a PS/2 keyboard and a serial port, which boots in 74 to 94 ms. A Python script converts the published weights once into a 613.66 MiB Q8_0 file. On an AMD EPYC 7642 the author measures 20.70 tokens per second on one thread and 125.86 on 40, and states 18 to 36% faster decoding than llama.cpp at Q8_0, with the prompt read one token at a time where llama.cpp reads it in batches; the kernel reaches 134.9 tokens per second under KVM. Its greedy output matches PyTorch on 64 of 64 tokens. The figures are the author's own.
- [MeMo trains a small model on question-answer pairs drawn from a corpus and lets the main model question it in place of a search index; it leads retrieval on long narratives and ties it on web questions, at 240 to 420 GPU-hours per corpus](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-26-memo-memory-as-a-model.md): advice, paper, watch, 2026-11-26. MeMo: Memory as a Model (arXiv 2605.15156, May 2026), by nine authors from NUS, A*STAR, the University of Tokyo, Liquid AI, MIT CSAIL and the Singapore-MIT Alliance, replaces the retrieval index with a model. A 32B generator turns the corpus into question-answer pairs (about 0.7 to 1.6 million per corpus); a smaller model, Qwen2.5-14B in the main setting, is fully fine-tuned on them and never sees the documents; the main model, left unchanged, questions it in three stages. On NarrativeQA with Gemini 3 Flash as the main model, MeMo scores 53.58% against 26.62% for dense retrieval and 23.21% for graph retrieval; on BrowseComp-Plus graph retrieval scores 56.11% against MeMo's 54.22% with Qwen2.5-32B, and the two tie with Gemini. With added false documents, retrieval loses up to 6.22 points and MeMo stays level. Building one corpus's memory costs about 240 to 420 H200 GPU-hours. The figures are the authors' own.
- [Declare, a user-interface language written by models and checked by its compiler: half React's lines and eleven hidden checks of eleven in one run; Softanza measures Zayn and Haro's diagnostics the same way](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-24-declare-ui-language.md): advice, release, learn, 2026-11-24. Declare, by David Temkin (co-founder of Laszlo Systems, which made OpenLaszlo), is an MIT-licensed declarative language for user interfaces, described as a UI language for you and your AI. Square brackets hold the view tree and braces hold TypeScript; an attribute in braces is a constraint whose dependencies the compiler extracts, and an assignment makes its dependents recompute. There is no CSS. The same tree renders to the DOM, to a canvas or to a native Mac host, in Node or the browser with no build step. It ships an agent skill, a six-rung verifier, and diagnostics that each name the rewrite that fixes them. In the author's single-run comparison, a ticket-buying app took 1,279 lines against React's 2,666, and its first build that ran passed eleven hidden checks of eleven against React's six. The figures are the author's own.
- [Besimple post-trains two open speech models on medical terms for about $500 and beats three closed models on medical dictation; Softanza measures its own transcriber on the words of a domain](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-24-medical-asr-post-training.md): advice, practice, learn, 2026-11-24. On November 23, 2026 Baseten published how Besimple adapted two open speech recognition models, Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Qwen3-ASR, to medical vocabulary. From a dictionary of 274,541 terms they generated sentences, spoke them with synthetic voices of varied accents, replaced about 29% of those clips with human recordings over several rounds, and mixed in general speech: 813 hours in all, trained with LoRA for an estimated $500 of GPU time for both models. Errors on medical terms in human dictation fell from 2.83% to 0.87% for Nemotron and from 5.84% to 2.05% for Qwen3-ASR; the best closed model measured scored 1.05%. On general English speech the adapted models stay behind the closed ones, and Qwen3-ASR lost ground there. The figures are the authors' own.
- [Microsoft announces seven MAI models at Ignite, among them a coding model priced against GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 and a routing model built on Gemma 4; Softanza states the price basis of every comparison and measures its own router](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-24-microsoft-mai-ignite.md): advice, release, watch, 2026-11-24. At Ignite on November 17, 2026, Microsoft AI announced seven models: MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash for coding, MAI Cyber 2 Flash for security defence, MAI Image 2.7 and MAI Image 2.7 Flash, MAI Realtime 1 for live speech to speech, and Microsoft Decision 1.1 for routing requests inside applications. Microsoft states that MAI Code 2 reaches 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of the cost and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5's at 5%, averaged over four coding benchmarks, with MAI Code 2's cost taken at its 50% promotional price. MAI Realtime 1 is priced at $0.01 per audio minute. Decision 1.1 is built on Gemma 4 26B A4B and is described as 50 times faster and 79 times cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol. The coding models are in GitHub Copilot; none of the seven is released as open weights. The figures are Microsoft's own.
- [Anthropic interviews 58 companies: AI's value comes from more output and from roles rebuilt around a whole workflow, and the bottleneck is review; Softanza's Foundry states the review each pack creates](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-24-working-with-ai-interviews.md): advice, paper, learn, 2026-11-24. On November 23, 2026 Anthropic's economics team (Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory) published Working with AI, a study of 66 face-to-face interviews in 58 US companies adopting AI, covering nearly 300 applications. Most of the value interviewees reported came from more output rather than lower cost, and around half of the output gains came from doing existing work faster. The largest gains came with broad change: one person or team owning a whole workflow, and staff moved to the tasks that hold work up. The bottlenecks named were inside the companies, above all the load of reviewing what AI produces and uneven adoption. Two-thirds of the companies reported hiring less because of AI, 10 reported hiring more, and two saw a position fully automated away. The authors describe the study as qualitative, with value as the interviewees describe it.
- [Google gives Agent Substrate 1.0 and gVisor to the CNCF: an agent holds no credential, and the gateway adds it outside the sandbox; Softanza reads its credential broker against that line](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-23-agent-substrate-gvisor.md): advice, release, learn, 2026-11-23. On November 5, 2026 Google Cloud announced the donation of Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, with Agent Substrate at version 1.0 under Apache-2.0. Each agent session, called an actor, runs in its own gVisor sandbox or Cloud Hypervisor microVM on Kubernetes, with its own files, memory and network rules; plain Linux containers are refused. Networking is deny by default, and an actor holds no API key or cloud token: an egress gateway outside the sandbox adds the credential to each approved outbound request. An idle actor is snapshotted and its slot freed; the project reports a resume in under 500 ms and more than 500 activations per second. The figures are the project's own.
- [OpenAI describes the sandbox of its coding agent: rules by the operating system, a tool server outside them by default, and deny patterns read once at start; Softanza checks its own rules at each access](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-23-codex-sandbox-profiles.md): advice, practice, learn, 2026-11-23. On November 18, 2026 OpenAI published an engineering account of the sandbox in Codex, its coding agent. Shell commands run under the operating system's own mechanisms: Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap with seccomp-bpf on Linux, and a Microsoft sandbox on Windows. The built-in workspace profile allows writes inside the workspace, keeps the .git and .codex folders read-only, and closes the network; an optional proxy applies allow and deny rules by domain. The article states three bounds in its own words: a tool server started over standard input and output runs outside the sandbox by default, deny patterns are expanded when the sandbox starts so a file created later is outside them, and name lookups can carry data out.
- [A small on-device agent that decided correctly several times is more likely to allow what its policy forbids; Softanza's governed actor decides each act apart from the model](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-23-correct-precedents-small-agents.md): advice, paper, defend, 2026-11-23. In 'Correct Precedents Induce Policy Violations in On-Device LLM Agents' (arXiv 2611.27216, November 20, 2026) Chong Tian and co-authors study small agents that run on a device and hand some work to a cloud model under restrictions. They find that correct earlier decisions in a session make a later violation more likely, an effect they name correct-precedent generalization: in 13 open-weight models from nine developers, and a single correct precedent can roughly halve the safe rate of the most affected agent. Their remedy, Paired Decision Distillation, trains a small adapter on the decisions of a weakly affected teacher and restores the safe rate to nearly 100% in every distilled model, with no added prompt text or model call. The abstract was read; the figures are the authors'.
- [A study of four coding agents finds that a rules file is advice and a gate is a decision: agents crossed a written boundary in 7 of 45 runs without a gate; Softanza gives each rule that matters a gate](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-23-rules-file-is-not-a-gate.md): advice, paper, learn, 2026-11-23. In 'Markdown Is Not a Firewall' (arXiv 2611.27112, November 20, 2026) Sandeep Dhuri gives one 278-word rules file to four coding agents, Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and OpenCode, on 20 small repositories with hidden tests and four planted boundaries: a refused endpoint, a destructive shortcut, a planted instruction and a planted package. With no gate in front of the forbidden service, 7 of 45 runs reached it. Behind a gate that blocks and logs, agents tried to cross a boundary in 5 of 90 steps. The file also had a cost: one agent's hidden-test pass rate fell from 99.0% to 67.7% with it, and in 11 of its 36 steps it reported completion while under half the tests passed. The abstract was read; the figures are the author's.
- [Small open models asked to quote the page that proves each answer reach 84.5% on company filings, and 16 to 167 wrong answers in 1,000 pass every automatic check; Softanza counts the same on its own set](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-23-small-models-checkable-evidence.md): advice, paper, learn, 2026-11-23. In 'Show Your Work' (arXiv 2611.24990, November 18, 2026) Krishna Nandula publishes Filing-Evidence: 1,000 questions over 90 annual and quarterly filings of 45 United States companies, with answer keys taken from the filings' own machine-readable tags. Each answer must give a page and a verbatim quote, which a program checks. Ten open models of 7 to 21 billion parameters ran on one RTX 4090. Accuracy with checkable evidence ran from 17.1% to 82.7% in the plain setup, and the best result was 84.5%, by Qwen3.5-9B. Between 16 and 167 answers per 1,000 were wrong and passed every automatic check; 57% of those were errors of scale or unit. Retrying after a failed check added up to 3.9 points. Code and data are public. The abstract was read; the figures are the author's.
- [GPUOS runs background work beside a latency-bound model on one GPU by making it yield at checkpoints; Softanza learns the yield rule for its own GPU jobs](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-15-gpuos-shared-gpu.md): advice, paper, learn, 2026-11-15. GPUOS is an MIT research prototype from the Multi-V-VM group, described as sharing a GPU without NVIDIA's MIG or MPS. Its code keeps one persistent kernel running on the GPU with a work queue, replaces operators at run time through a table of device function pointers, and merges many tiny operations into one compiled batch. Its working-draft paper, pushed on November 12, 2026, builds on OpenInfer's 'The GPU Needs an Operating System' and specifies restartable tasks admitted under revocable resource leases. On one RTX 5090, background work that yields every 4 tiles costs a streaming foreground 0.62% at the 99th percentile, against 23.68% when it never yields. The authors state that the measurements support selected mechanisms.
- [Tur serves eight requests from one small model at six times the speed of one by reading the weights once per step; Softanza measures the same rule on its own decoder](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-15-tur-metal-inference.md): advice, release, learn, 2026-11-15. Tur, by Danylo Kravchenko, is an Apache-2.0 inference engine in Rust for Apple Silicon Macs: one binary for generation, an OpenAI-compatible server, Whisper transcription and quantization, on Metal kernels and the Candle framework. Its continuous batching packs every request's next token into one pass, so the weights are read once for all of them: on an M3 Pro, Qwen3.5-0.8B at 8 bits decodes 123 tokens per second for one sequence and 729 for eight, against llama.cpp's 113 and 456. It plans all memory before loading a weight, keeps most experts of a mixture-of-experts model on the SSD behind a fixed cache, reuses shared prefixes, and drafts tokens from the prompt's own text. Figures are the author's.
- [Google's TPU Sync moves a model's working memory between chip, host memory, disk and network; Softanza manages its small models' state as one memory budget](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-14-google-tpu-sync.md): advice, release, learn, 2026-11-14. On November 9, 2026 Google Cloud announced TPU Sync, an open-source C++ library with PyTorch and JAX bindings that treats a TPU's on-chip memory, the host's pinned memory, shared storage and the data-centre network as one hierarchy for a model's key-value cache and weights. Tensors keep the chip's own layout at every level and move by direct memory access while the chip computes. In Google's lab test of July 2026 on TPU v7x, serving Qwen3 235B with prefill and decode on separate nodes, the median transfer of the cache fell from several seconds to about 230 ms and time to first token fell by 60% on average; with prefix caching on 64K-token contexts it reports up to 90% lower time to first token.
- [llmgw puts one gateway in front of an organisation's own GPUs; Softanza learns its priority bands and its residency rule](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-14-llmgw-gateway.md): advice, release, learn, 2026-11-14. llmgw, by Ilker Manap, is a gateway in one Go binary for organisations that run language models on their own GPU clusters: one OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoint over vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp and TensorRT-LLM, with tenants, keys, budgets, guardrails, per-tenant knowledge bases and a three-machine high-availability setup. Its README, at version 0.16.3 of November 3, 2026, reports that the gateway adds 0.15 to 0.49 ms at the 99th percentile with authentication and guardrail patterns on, measured on loopback, and that with admission control interactive latency stays within 1.24 times idle while 500 batch requests run, against 58 times without. It is published under the Functional Source License, which becomes Apache 2.0 after two years.
- [NVIDIA FLARE 2.9.1 admits a site to shared training only after its hardware and software match what all parties approved; Softanza's federation learns the admission rule](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-14-nvidia-flare-confidential.md): advice, release, learn, 2026-11-14. NVIDIA FLARE 2.9.1, released on November 12, 2026 under Apache-2.0, adds confidential computing as an optional technical preview to its federated-learning framework. Training runs inside confidential virtual machines or confidential containers on Intel TDX or AMD SEV-SNP, with or without NVIDIA confidential GPUs, on a site's own servers, on Kubernetes or on Azure, all in one federation. The application's image, code, configuration and secrets sit in an encrypted vault whose key the Trustee key broker releases only after the machine's measured boot matches approved reference values. Sites then check each other's evidence at registration and periodically; a site that fails is refused or quarantined.
- [OpenInfer measures a serving GPU's math units busy 6 to 11% of the time and schedules the rest; Softanza gives its one GPU a single owner](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-14-openinfer-gpu-os.md): advice, paper, learn, 2026-11-14. In 'The GPU Needs an Operating System' (arXiv 2611.08720, November 5, 2026), Reza Nourai and Behnam Bastani of OpenInfer measure two large open models served with stock vLLM on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell cards: the tensor units are active 6 to 11% of the time while kernels occupy the GPU about 94% of it, because each decoding step waits on memory. They propose a scheduler that lends idle parts of the chip to background work in pieces of 20 microseconds or less. With NVIDIA's static partitions, work written to share adds about a quarter of a GPU at a 5% slower decode step; their research kernel, running Llama-3.1-8B, adds the same at 0.3 to 1.6%.
- [llama.cpp and ggml reach version 1.0.0 with a versioning promise; Softanza moves its engine's ggml to the stable line](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-13-llama-cpp-v1.md): advice, release, adopt, 2026-11-13. On November 13, 2026 the ggml-org team at Hugging Face released llama.cpp v1.0.0 and ggml v1.0.0, three and a half years after the project began. Both libraries now follow semantic versioning: a breaking change to the public C API in their include folders raises the major version, a compatible feature, backend update or new model raises the minor, a bug fix raises the patch. To get there, llama.h loses 35 deprecated functions and ggml loses its deprecated API and the legacy DIAG_MASK operations. The release also adds FP8 key-value caches, an unbuffered model load on Windows, three text architectures, and fixes in llama-server for SSRF, CORS and DNS rebinding.
- [A small recogniser trained on synthetic Arabic words reads words it never saw; Softanza trains its Arabic recogniser the same way](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-13-trocr-arabic-synthetic.md): advice, practice, learn, 2026-11-13. An engineer reports fine-tuning Microsoft's TrOCR-Small, a 61-million-parameter recogniser of single printed text lines trained on English receipts, into an Arabic word reader: 78,000 unique Arabic words rendered into about 900,000 synthetic images with realistic augmentation, 80 minutes on one RTX 3090, 97.6% exact-word accuracy on vocabulary held out of training and 77.3% on photographs of street signs. TrOCR pairs an image Transformer encoder with a text Transformer decoder, scores 95.86 F1 on SROIE in its small size, and reads one line at a time.
- [NVIDIA SkillSpector scans an agent skill before it is installed; Softanza checks its agent files the same way](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-12-nvidia-skillspector.md): advice, release, learn, 2026-11-12. NVIDIA SkillSpector is an open-source (Apache 2.0) scanner for the skills that coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI install, at v2.13.4 on November 4, 2026. It checks a skill from a directory, a file, a zip, a URL or a Git repository against 71 patterns in 17 categories, among them prompt injection, data exfiltration, excessive agency, memory poisoning and MCP tool poisoning, first by static analysis and optionally by a language model, and reports a 0-100 risk score in terminal, JSON, Markdown or SARIF. Its README cites a study of 31,132 marketplace skills in which 26.1% held at least one vulnerability and 5.2% showed likely malicious intent.
- [Rayline's ARC: an open 0.8B model that picks the model for each step of an agent; Softanza learns its local-first escalation](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-12-rayline-arc.md): advice, release, learn, 2026-11-12. On November 11, 2026 Rayline Labs announced ARC 1.0, an open-weight (Apache 2.0) routing model built on Qwen3.5-0.8B. For each step of an agent it predicts, per candidate model, the probability of success and the tokens the step will bill, then a policy weighs that success against the prices the application supplies; a question head answers developer-defined yes/no, choice and score questions with probabilities. On six benchmarks Rayline reports that ARC, routing between Opus 5.5 and a locally served DeepSeek model, keeps 97.5% of Opus 5.5's quality at 92.9% lower cost.
- [Samsung's LittleBit stores a model's weights in under one bit each; Softanza weighs memory against quality on its small models](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-12-samsung-littlebit.md): advice, paper, watch, 2026-11-12. LittleBit, from Samsung Research (NeurIPS 2025; fifth version February 5, 2026), compresses a language model's weights to between 0.1 and 1 bit per weight by factoring each weight matrix into two low-rank matrices of signs with three scaling vectors, plus a residual path of the same shape, trained against the original model. The paper reports Llama2-13B in under 0.9 GB at 0.1 bits per weight, about 31 times smaller than 16-bit, and a speedup of up to 11.6 times on one layer with its GPU kernel. Its code, with the follow-up LittleBit-2 (ICML 2026), is published under the non-commercial CC BY-NC 4.0 licence.
- [A2UI 1.0: an open protocol for agents to answer with a native screen; Zane gives it intent and law, and a projection to it](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-11-a2ui-1-0.md): advice, release, correct, 2026-11-11. On November 11, 2026 the A2UI project, started at Google, released A2UI 1.0 under Apache 2.0: a streaming protocol in which an agent sends a screen as data, built only from components the app registered in a locked catalog, and each app draws it with its own native components in React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI and soon Jetpack Compose. Version 1.0 adds typed function calls in both directions, components from several catalogs on one screen, and A2UI Express, which its authors say describes the same screen in about three times fewer output tokens than JSON. Gemini, Atlassian and ByteDance ship it.
- [Liquid AI's LFM3: six 2B-class models on one backbone, built for the device; Softanza learns from its decision models](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-11-liquid-lfm3.md): advice, release, learn, 2026-11-11. On October 27, 2026 Liquid AI released LFM3, six open-weight models of about 2 billion parameters each (text, vision with video, audio with speech output, omni, and two d1 decision models), all branched from one 1.7B base. The base mixes 13 gated short-convolution layers with 5 sliding-window and 6 global attention layers, fits in about 1 GB at 4 bits, reads 256K tokens and covers 16 languages, Arabic and French among them. The d1 models answer a list of questions about one input in a single forward pass, each answer with a calibrated probability.
- [NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B: a 4 GB model for local agents; Softanza adds its Gemma 4 family and takes it to the model court](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-11-nemotron-bolt-e4b.md): advice, release, adopt, 2026-11-11. On October 23, 2026 NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B, a small language model post-trained by reinforcement learning from Google's Gemma 4 E4B for multi-turn tool use, instruction following and grounding. It has 8 billion parameters, 4 billion of them effective, a 64K-token context, and ships as a 4 GB Q4_K_M GGUF file for llama.cpp with a companion DFlash drafter for speculative decoding. Its weights, training data and recipes are published under the OpenMDW-1.1 licence, and NVIDIA's own benchmark table puts it ahead of Gemma 4 E4B on most of 21 agent and instruction tests.
- [NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Embed 1B finds pages by text or by image in 34 languages; Softanza measures it on Arabic and French retrieval](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-11-nemotron-embed-1b.md): advice, release, watch, 2026-11-11. On October 20, 2026 NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Embed 1B, an embedding model that turns a query, a passage or the image of a document page into one vector, for retrieval across text, tables, charts and infographics. NVIDIA evaluated text retrieval in 34 languages, Arabic, French and Persian among them, and image retrieval in 18; its vectors can be cut to 1024 or 512 dimensions and stay usable once normalised. It is published under OpenMDW-1.1, with an NVFP4 variant for recent NVIDIA GPUs.
- [NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Parse reads a page into text, tables and layout with 0.63 billion parameters; Softanza's OCR court hears it](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-11-nemotron-parse.md): advice, release, learn, 2026-11-11. On October 17, 2026 NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a 0.631-billion-parameter model that turns a page image into text, tables, chart data, reading order, semantic classes and bounding boxes, exported as Markdown, HTML or JSON. NVIDIA reports 75.20 on the ParseBench benchmark in its three-pass mode, the best of the systems it compares, and multilingual OCR evaluated over 163 language and script entries. On November 4 it added a native 89.3-million-parameter DFlash2 drafter for speculative decoding; the model is published under OpenMDW-1.1.
- [NVIDIA OpenShell governs an agent from outside its process; Softanza adds that boundary to the rules it already decides in code](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-11-nvidia-openshell.md): advice, release, learn, 2026-11-11. NVIDIA OpenShell is an open-source (Apache 2.0) runtime for AI agents, at v0.1.8 on November 10, 2026, and moving to the CNCF. Each agent runs in a sandbox whose files, system calls and network are confined by the kernel, a supervisor outside the agent checks every outbound request against a deny-by-default policy and adds real credentials only to requests bound for approved endpoints, and a prover uses formal logic to show what new access a policy change would grant before it is applied. It runs on Linux, on macOS with Apple Silicon, and on Windows through WSL 2 or Microsoft MXC.
- [NVIDIA Snapshot restores a warmed-up GPU inference worker in seconds; Softanza saves the warm state it pays for, a read prompt](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-11-nvidia-snapshot.md): advice, release, correct, 2026-11-11. On November 8, 2026 NVIDIA released Snapshot v0.3.0, an open-source (Apache 2.0) Kubernetes system that checkpoints a fully initialised GPU inference pod, CPU and GPU memory together, and restores it on another node instead of starting it again. It combines CRIU for the process with NVIDIA's cuda-checkpoint for the GPU, and works with vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM. On NVIDIA's own B200 tests, restore was 8.1 to 35.9 times faster than a cold start across 22 configurations, for example 4.7 seconds against 104 seconds for Qwen3-0.6B on vLLM.
- [NVIDIA ships a small drafter with each new model and speeds up llama.cpp; Softanza takes the algorithm into its own decoder](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-11-speculative-decoding-dflash.md): advice, practice, correct, 2026-11-11. On September 3, 2026 NVIDIA said its work with the llama.cpp and vLLM communities gives up to 1.9 times higher local throughput on a GeForce RTX 5090, from GPU kernel work, better speculative decoding and faster prefill. Since then its new models ship with a small DFlash drafter, which llama.cpp's official server runs, and its open-source C++ runtime TensorRT Edge-LLM (0.11.1, October 28) added the Bolt E4B drafter and TensorRT for RTX on Windows. Most of the speed comes from CUDA code for NVIDIA's newest GPUs; the speculative-decoding algorithm itself is portable.
- [Radar runs for any project: one file says what its agent learns and watches](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-09-lookout-for-any-project.md): info, feature, adopt, 2026-11-09. Radar now reads everything that belongs to its project from one file, radar.yaml: the project, the watch, its readers, its map, and what the watching agent learns before each survey. The feed, the site with its trends, and the bar take their names and texts from it, and version 1.1.0 of the bar reads any watch's feed with the key the page gives it.
- [A coding agent's "don't ask again" writes secrets into a file that gets published](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-08-agent-approvals-leak-secrets.md): action, security, defend, 2026-11-08. Apiiro reports that when a Claude Code user approves a command with "Yes, and don't ask again", the exact command, including any password or key typed into it, is saved as a permission rule in .claude/settings.local.json inside the project. The file is kept out of git only by the developer's global ignore list, not by the repository's own .gitignore, and Apiiro counted 1,122 public copies on GitHub holding a real secret, out of 104,185.
- [Radar's feed is signed: check it came from this repository unchanged](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-08-feed-signing.md): info, feature, adopt, 2026-11-08. Radar publishes an SSH signature beside each feed file, feed/index.json.sig and feed/feed.json.sig, made with one Ed25519 key kept for this purpose by Radar's maintainer. Any reader with OpenSSH can check a feed with ssh-keygen against the public key and the namespace radar-feed. The change adds files and adds nothing to the feed itself, so the feed stays at version 1; docs/FEED.md gives the key, its fingerprint and the command.
- [GitHub will block pull_request_target in public repositories from December 2](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-08-github-blocks-pull-request-target.md): info, practice, adopt, 2026-11-08. GitHub announced on November 2, 2026 that from December 2, 2026, GitHub Actions blocks pull_request_target events by default in every public repository unless an Actions event policy allows them. Enforcement is tried in two windows, November 9 and November 16, 16:00 to 18:00 UTC. Private and internal repositories are not affected.
- [Code repaired by a model after an API change can pass its checks and still be wrong](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-08-llm-repairs-pass-wrong.md): advice, paper, adopt, 2026-11-08. A study submitted on November 5, 2026 looks at code that models repair after documented changes in CPython, Node.js and SQLite. Repairs that run cleanly can still give wrong answers: a gate built on typical inputs let 41% of the wrong repairs through, and adding one input written from the release note cut that to 6.5%. The expected outputs came from the old program on the old runtime.
- [Radar opens: a public watch on AI, read from Softanza's point of view](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-08-lookout-opens.md): info, idea, adopt, 2026-11-08. Softanza opened Radar, a public repository that reads developments in AI at their source and judges each one against what Softanza builds. Every entry is written twice in one file, as a page for people and as data for programs, and a feed is generated from the data.
- [Two MCP clients let a malicious server obtain a token meant for another server](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-08-mcp-oauth-resource-check.md): advice, security, defend, 2026-11-08. Two advisories published on November 5, 2026 describe the same flaw in two MCP clients, the Go SDK mcp-go before 1.2.1 and the ChatCLI agent before 1.215.2: the client took the resource named in a server's protected resource metadata without checking that it matched the server it had connected to. A malicious MCP server could name another server on the same authorization server, have the user sign in, and replay the token it received.
- [SPILLWAY: an agent may act only on targets that came from a trusted, typed field](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-08-spillway-target-admission.md): advice, paper, learn, 2026-11-08. A paper submitted on November 4, 2026 proposes a defence for tool-using agents against prompt injection that does not rely on a model: a call with side effects is admitted only if every target it names that is not in the user's request was returned in a typed identity field, such as an email address or a channel, by a read-only tool. A rule-based sanitizer removes instruction-like text, and a local model reviews only the calls the rule refused. The authors report no successful in-scope attack across twelve benchmark settings.
- [A prompt library ran any function a template named: tools must come from a registry](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-08-tool-paths-from-prompts-run-code.md): advice, security, learn, 2026-11-08. The Python prompt library banks, up to version 2.4.2, read a tool's import path from the text of a prompt template and imported and called whatever it named when the model asked for that tool (CVE-2026-61536, high). Whoever could write a template, in a shared registry or a fetched prompt, could run code in the application. Version 2.4.3 resolves tools only from a registry filled at render time.
- [Zig 0.17.1 fixes the blockers of 0.17.0; Softanza measures the move from 0.15.2](https://mayouni.github.io/stzradar/items/2026/2026-11-08-zig-0-17-1.md): advice, release, watch, 2026-11-08. Zig 0.17.1 is a bug-fix release that addresses more than 57 issues reported after 0.17.0, chiefly regressions and upgrade blockers; the project says most users who could not move to 0.17.0 should be able to move to 0.17.1. Its news page dates it November 3, 2026 and its download page November 2.
